articles.title: LIVE on August 4: Narratives about Indigenous Rights – Whose stories are being told  across media ecosystems?
articles.summary: Join us on August 4th to explore how narratives about Indigenous Right are being discussed and framed in traditional and online media.
articles.content:
Indigenous rights are often reported on, but less often reported by the Indigenous communities struggling to exercise their rights, whether related to their land, access to resources, language and culture, and the right to freedom of expression and access to information.

Join us for a Global Voices Insights webinar to explore how narratives about Indigenous rights are framed in the mainstream and digital media around the world, and the importance of agency in telling their own stories and framing their own issues. This webinar will be part of Global Voices’ August Spotlight: Indigenous Rights, which explores how Indigenous communities around the world are finding ways to assert their rights through different mechanisms, including legal challenges, community organizing and activism, and other ways to creatively resist.

We’ll hear from Indigenous experts who have a local understanding of these conversations about how Indigenous rights are discussed and portrayed within local, national, and global media ecosystems, and their own work to promote greater self-representation through journalism, advocacy, storytelling, and media literacy.

Join us on YouTube on August 4th, at 1:00 pm UTC (4:00 pm Kenya / 4:00 pm Latvia / 6:45 pm Nepal) for this discussion featuring:

Lucas Kasosi is an Indigenous Maasai journalist and communications professional from Kenya. His work focuses on Indigenous rights, self-representation, traditional knowledge, environmental justice, and community-led storytelling. Through journalism and Indigenous media, Lucas works to amplify community voices and challenge narratives about Indigenous peoples that are often shaped without their participation. His work has been published by Cultural Survival and other platforms, covering Indigenous rights, climate justice, conservation, and cultural identity.

Barsha Lekhi works at the intersection of climate change, biodiversity conservation, and Indigenous peoples, with over seven years of experience across UNESCO, UNDP, and Indigenous organizations in Nepal and across Asia. Currently, she serves as Project Officer/Indigenous Engagement Specialist at UNESCO Nepal, leading the Local and Indigenous Knowledge Systems Program and working alongside government ministries, civil society, and Indigenous communities. Her work has taken her from community consultations in Nepal to international climate negotiations at UNFCCC COP in Egypt, Dubai, and Baku. She holds a master’s degree in environmental sciences from Jawaharlal Nehru University, India, and a personal commitment to the principle that no one should be left behind not in climate/biodiversity policy, not in development planning, and not in the conversations that shape our collective future.

Valts Ernštreits is an Indigenous researcher, poet, and visual artist who has worked for decades at the intersection of language revitalization, self-representation, and Indigenous rights advocacy for Latvia’s small Indigenous Livonian community — successfully building spaces for Livonian-language use, education, and digital and media presence, and driving community activism rooted in community perspectives. His work also spans educating wider society and promoting Livonian-related themes and heritage across all levels of the education system, as well as through media and state policy. Actively engaged in advocacy and knowledge-sharing on both sides of the dialogue — working from within the Indigenous community while also serving on councils and institutions shaping governmental media policy and its implementation — his perspective offers hands-on insight into the complex realities as viewed from both sides of the contact line.

articles.personality_title: Indigenous voices lead conversation on media and rights in global webinar
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Indigenous rights are often talked about in the news, but rarely by Indigenous people themselves. These rights include control over their land, culture, language, and the freedom to share their own stories.

**What happened** – On August 4th, a free online webinar will bring together Indigenous experts from Kenya, Nepal, and Latvia. They will discuss how Indigenous stories are told in traditional and online media, and why it is important for Indigenous communities to tell their own stories. The event is part of Global Voices’ August Spotlight on Indigenous Rights.

**Impact** – This webinar is important because it gives Indigenous people a chance to explain their views directly, rather than having others speak for them. Experts like Lucas Kasosi, Barsha Lekhi, and Valts Ernštreits work to protect Indigenous languages, promote environmental justice, and support Indigenous self-representation in media. Their voices help change how the world understands Indigenous issues.

**What’s next step** – The discussion will be streamed live on YouTube, allowing people everywhere to listen and learn. It may inspire more Indigenous communities to share their stories and encourage media outlets to include Indigenous voices more fairly.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Indigenous experts are leading a global conversation to reshape how their rights and stories are shared in the media.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les voix indigènes dirigent la conversation sur les médias et les droits lors d’un webinaire mondial
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les droits des peuples indigènes sont souvent évoqués dans les médias, mais rarement par les indigènes eux-mêmes. Ces droits concernent le contrôle de leurs terres, cultures, langues et la liberté de raconter leurs propres histoires.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 4 août, un webinaire en ligne gratuit réunira des experts indigènes du Kenya, du Népal et de la Lettonie. Ils discuteront de la manière dont les histoires indigènes sont racontées dans les médias traditionnels et en ligne, et pourquoi il est important que les communautés indigènes racontent elles-mêmes leurs récits. Cet événement fait partie du Focus d’août de Global Voices sur les droits indigènes.

**Impact** – Ce webinaire est important car il donne aux indigènes la possibilité d’expliquer directement leurs points de vue, plutôt que de laisser d’autres parler à leur place. Des experts comme Lucas Kasosi, Barsha Lekhi et Valts Ernštreits travaillent à protéger les langues indigènes, à promouvoir la justice environnementale et à soutenir l’auto-représentation indigène dans les médias. Leurs voix aident à changer la façon dont le monde comprend les enjeux indigènes.

**Étape suivante** – La discussion sera diffusée en direct sur YouTube, permettant à tout le monde d’écouter et d’apprendre. Cela pourrait encourager davantage de communautés indigènes à partager leurs histoires et inciter les médias à inclure plus justement ces voix.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des experts indigènes mènent une conversation mondiale pour transformer la manière dont leurs droits et histoires sont partagés dans les médias.
articles.personality_title_es: Voces indígenas lideran conversación sobre medios y derechos en seminario web global
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los derechos indígenas se hablan mucho en las noticias, pero rara vez son contados por los propios indígenas. Estos derechos incluyen el control sobre sus tierras, cultura, idioma y la libertad de contar sus propias historias.

**Qué pasó** – El 4 de agosto, un seminario web gratuito en línea reunirá a expertos indígenas de Kenia, Nepal y Letonia. Hablarán sobre cómo se cuentan las historias indígenas en medios tradicionales y digitales, y por qué es importante que las comunidades indígenas cuenten sus propias historias. Este evento es parte del Enfoque de agosto de Global Voices sobre los Derechos Indígenas.

**Impacto** – Este seminario es importante porque permite a los indígenas explicar sus puntos de vista directamente, en lugar de que otros hablen por ellos. Expertos como Lucas Kasosi, Barsha Lekhi y Valts Ernštreits trabajan para proteger los idiomas indígenas, promover la justicia ambiental y apoyar la auto-representación indígena en los medios. Sus voces ayudan a cambiar cómo el mundo entiende los temas indígenas.

**Próximo paso** – La charla será transmitida en vivo por YouTube, permitiendo que personas de todo el mundo escuchen y aprendan. Esto puede inspirar a más comunidades indígenas a compartir sus historias y animar a los medios a incluir mejor las voces indígenas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Expertos indígenas lideran una conversación global para cambiar cómo se comparten sus derechos e historias en los medios.

articles.title: Amelia Dimoldenberg: I wouldn't invite Andy Burnham on Chicken Shop Date - but I'd love a chat
articles.summary: The YouTube star on helping young creatives, and who she wants (and doesn’t want) on her show.
articles.content:
I meet Dimoldenberg not in a chicken shop, but in a studio in BBC Broadcasting House in central London. She's OK with that though ("I love the pot plants," she says. "It's fantastic. I'm very happy to be here.")

It's been more than a decade since she set up Chicken Shop Date. Since then, she's interviewed everyone from Cher to Ed Sheeran, and has become a celebrity in her own right.

The show is based around her trademark dry, awkward flirting style. In person, I find her inscrutable. You get the sense she's judging your questions (I was secretly relieved when she told me later they were great).

But she visibly lights up when talking about her free summer course, the Dimz Inc. Academy, which she launched to train up people aged 18-24 and help them get into the creative industries.

The course offers guaranteed paid work placements, mentoring and an opportunity to gain experience across digital media. She is now bringing it back for a second year, and has extended it from one week to four.

"I started Chicken Shop Date as part of a youth club, and we made a magazine, and everything I learned there, the connections I made, the mentoring I got, set me up for the career that I have today," she explains.

"So it was always such a big ambition of mine to be able to give that back to young people when I was able to."

Behind it is a serious issue. Dimoldenberg points to the high number of young people not in employment, education or training - a group known as Neets.

"That's really a big crisis. So there is no better time to be trying to do what I can to support the next generation of young people," she says.

She added that while Burnham may not be welcome on her YouTube series, she would "100% love to have a conversation with him" about what he's doing to tackle youth unemployment.

"I think having more training schemes, apprenticeships is really, really vital in helping young people," she says.

articles.personality_title: YouTube star Amelia Dimoldenberg helps young people into creative jobs
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Amelia Dimoldenberg is known for her YouTube show Chicken Shop Date, where she interviews celebrities with a funny and awkward style. She started the show over ten years ago and has become well-known for it.

**What happened** – Amelia has created a free summer course called the Dimz Inc. Academy to help young people aged 18 to 24 get jobs in creative industries. The course offers paid work placements, mentoring, and hands-on experience in digital media. After the first successful year, she is expanding the program from one week to four weeks.

**Impact** – This program helps tackle a big problem: many young people are not working or studying, which makes it hard for them to start careers. By giving them real work experience and support, Amelia’s course gives these young people a better chance to find creative jobs and build their futures.

**What's next step** – Amelia will run the course again this summer with more weeks and places. She also wants to talk with leaders like Andy Burnham about ways to create more training and apprenticeships for young people.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Amelia Dimoldenberg uses her experience and platform to create a free program that gives young people real opportunities in the creative world.
articles.personality_title_fr: La star de YouTube Amelia Dimoldenberg aide les jeunes à trouver un emploi dans la création
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Amelia Dimoldenberg est connue pour son émission YouTube Chicken Shop Date, où elle interviewe des célébrités avec un style drôle et maladroit. Elle a lancé l’émission il y a plus de dix ans et elle est devenue célèbre grâce à cela.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Amelia a créé un cours d’été gratuit appelé Dimz Inc. Academy pour aider les jeunes de 18 à 24 ans à trouver un emploi dans les métiers créatifs. Le cours offre des stages rémunérés, du mentorat et une expérience pratique dans les médias numériques. Après une première année réussie, elle étend le programme d’une à quatre semaines.

**Impact** – Ce programme aide à résoudre un grand problème : beaucoup de jeunes ne travaillent pas et ne suivent pas de formation, ce qui complique leur entrée dans la vie professionnelle. En leur offrant une vraie expérience de travail et du soutien, le cours d’Amelia donne à ces jeunes une meilleure chance de trouver un emploi créatif et de construire leur avenir.

**Prochaine étape** – Amelia organisera à nouveau le cours cet été avec plus de semaines et de places. Elle souhaite aussi discuter avec des responsables comme Andy Burnham pour créer plus de formations et d’apprentissages pour les jeunes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Amelia Dimoldenberg utilise son expérience et sa notoriété pour créer un programme gratuit qui offre de vraies opportunités aux jeunes dans le monde créatif.
articles.personality_title_es: La estrella de YouTube Amelia Dimoldenberg ayuda a jóvenes a encontrar trabajos creativos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Amelia Dimoldenberg es conocida por su programa de YouTube Chicken Shop Date, donde entrevista a celebridades con un estilo divertido y torpe. Comenzó el programa hace más de diez años y se ha hecho famosa por ello.

**Qué pasó** – Amelia creó un curso de verano gratuito llamado Dimz Inc. Academy para ayudar a jóvenes de 18 a 24 años a conseguir trabajos en industrias creativas. El curso ofrece prácticas pagadas, mentoría y experiencia práctica en medios digitales. Tras un primer año exitoso, ampliará el programa de una a cuatro semanas.

**Impacto** – Este programa ayuda a enfrentar un gran problema: muchos jóvenes no trabajan ni estudian, lo que dificulta que comiencen sus carreras. Al darles experiencia real y apoyo, el curso de Amelia les da una mejor oportunidad para encontrar trabajos creativos y construir su futuro.

**Próximo paso** – Amelia organizará el curso nuevamente este verano con más semanas y plazas. También quiere hablar con líderes como Andy Burnham para crear más programas de formación y aprendizajes para jóvenes.

**Frase clave** – Amelia Dimoldenberg usa su experiencia y plataforma para crear un programa gratuito que ofrece oportunidades reales a los jóvenes en el mundo creativo.
